title: Joining Multiple Tables
learningObjectives: Explain how a join chain combines data from three or more related tables.
Choose the correct key relationship for each join in a multi-table query.
Write readable queries using aliases and explicit ON conditions.
Combine multi-table joins with filtering and aggregation.
Preserve rows with LEFT JOIN when related records may be missing.

understand.concept: A multi-table join combines more than two tables by adding join operations to a query. Each join should connect tables through a valid relationship, commonly a primary-key and foreign-key pair. In a many-to-many model, a junction table such as enrollments connects the two entity tables.
understand.whyItMatters: Real business questions often require facts spread across several normalized tables, such as students and their courses, orders and their products, or employees and departments.
understand.analogy: It is like following a chain of reference numbers across several related registers to assemble one useful record.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not show row multiplication, NULL extension, join order choices or the effect of an incorrect relationship condition.

examples.title: Inspect the three-table sample
examples.explanation: The sample separates student facts, course facts and the many-to-many enrollment relationship.

examples.title: Join students, enrollments and courses
examples.expectedOutput: Asha Rao | SQL; Asha Rao | Python; Bilal Khan | SQL
examples.explanation: Each join connects the next table through the appropriate key. The join chain returns one row per enrollment.

examples.title: Filter a multi-table result
examples.expectedOutput: Asha Rao | SQL; Bilal Khan | SQL
examples.explanation: The WHERE predicate filters the completed logical join result to one course.

examples.title: Count enrollments for every course
examples.explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps courses with no enrollment, and COUNT of a non-null enrollment key reports zero.

examples.title: Keep every student, including those without a course
examples.expectedOutput: Asha Rao | SQL; Asha Rao | Python; Bilal Khan | SQL; Chitra Das | NULL
examples.explanation: Each LEFT JOIN preserves the original student population through the chain.

practise.guidedTask: Run the setup and write the students-to-enrollments join first. Add the courses table only after the first relationship works. Compare your row count after each join.
practise.independentTask: Design a small orders, order_items and products schema. Insert at least three orders, four products and five line items. Write five multi-table queries, including one filtered report, one aggregate, one outer join and one query that identifies missing relationships.
hints: Map each foreign key to its referenced primary key.
Join the junction table between the two many-to-many entity tables.
Use COUNT of a non-null child key to count optional matches.
Test the query with one join at a time.

questions.prompt: What connects two tables in a join chain?
questions.explanation: Each ON clause specifies how the next table relates to the rows already in the query.

questions.prompt: Which table commonly connects two sides of a many-to-many relationship?
options: An index table with no keys
A duplicate copy of one entity
questions.explanation: The junction table stores references to both related entity tables.

questions.prompt: What can an incorrect or missing join condition cause?
questions.explanation: Without the correct relationship predicate, many or all row combinations may be returned.

questions.prompt: Which aggregate counts only matching enrollment rows after a LEFT JOIN?
questions.explanation: The non-null enrollment key is NULL for the placeholder row created by an unmatched LEFT JOIN.

questions.prompt: What is a good way to debug a complex multi-table join?
options: Add and verify one join at a time
Start with SELECT * from every table
Use DISTINCT to hide all extra rows
questions.answer: Add and verify one join at a time
questions.explanation: Incremental testing helps locate incorrect relationships and unexpected row multiplication.
